name: XR Guild
audience: The demo-night audience: enthusiasts, educators, and complete beginners who are curious about virtual and augmented reality and want to try it alongside other people. Deliberately broader than XR Guild's membership, which is working professionals across XR and spatial computing. Demo nights are open to anyone, free, with nothing to join. Members and non-members are equally expected at the door. They find XR Guild on Luma and LinkedIn and meet it in person at events held in bars and clubs.

visual.direction: Dark, roomy, and human. Cool indigo ground with one cyan signal, heavy geometric headlines, generous space, softened corners, and real photographs of people trying things. It should look like a good night in a dark room, not like a technology company.
colors: Cyan #5CE1F2 — accent, one use per surface
typography: Headline: Space Grotesk Bold, tracking -0.02em, fallback Arial Black then Helvetica
Labels and numbers: JetBrains Mono 400/500, tracking 0.08em, uppercase, fallback ui-monospace
imagery: Use: photographs of real people at real events — mid-demo, being handed a headset, laughing. Faces and hands.
Treatment: venue lighting as shot. Darken behind text rather than washing the image out. No heavy filters or grading toward the palette.
Avoid: product shots with nobody holding the headset, all stock photography, generic 3D grids and purple neon metaverse abstractions, and anyone who did not agree to be photographed.
Alternative when no photograph exists: the lens texture in brand/08-texture, as a background only.
visual.logo_usage: Master lockup is brand/01-logos/xr-guild-wordmark-stacked-cyan-on-indigo.svg. Clear space equals the height of the X on all four sides. Minimum 90px wide on screen for the stacked wordmark, 150px for the horizontal, 16px for the XR tile. Use the XR tile for square or small spaces. Never stretch, rotate, outline, recolour outside the palette, or fill the letterforms with texture or photography — the texture goes behind the mark. Never place another organisation's logo inside an XR Guild lockup.

do: Say what it costs — it is free, and that is the most important fact on the page
Say beginners are welcome, in those words
Name the date, time, and venue so they are readable across a bar
Carry all four parts of the invitation grammar: who this is, the invitation, where and when, and the no-barrier line
Use the real attendance number when quoting one
Describe membership plainly when it is the subject, in its own place — something to join, never something to be outside of
avoid: Implying that attending an event requires membership, approval, or an invitation — event-facing work must never read as exclusive
Attaching membership to an event invitation, or phrasing membership as a tier, level, or upgrade
Jargon or acronyms in public copy
Urgency and scarcity language such as limited spots or do not miss out
Omitting the no-barrier line to save space
Placing a venue or partner logo inside an XR Guild lockup
Promising attendee data to a sponsor — attendees are guests, not leads
Advertising language on behalf of a sponsor: comparative claims, pricing, endorsements, or a call to buy. Acknowledgement only
Photographing people who did not agree to it

cta_style: Invite a next step and name what it costs, which is nothing. Never urgency, scarcity, or pressure. Example: Grab a free spot on Luma. Turn up, try a headset, leave whenever you like.
notes: XR Guild is a 501(c)3 non-profit founded in 2022, volunteer-operated, with an existing identity at xrguild.org and a name carrying a registered mark. THIS BRAND SYSTEM IS A PROPOSED REFRESH, not approved identity — it requires sign-off from whoever owns brand decisions at the organisation before it is used as official. Two audiences that must not be conflated: demo nights are open to absolutely anyone, while membership is a separate deliberate choice. Lehman College / CUNY is a venue sometimes rented, not a sponsor or parent — credit hosts in XR Guild's own type, never with their logo. Sponsorship is acknowledgement, not advertising, and money documents carry the written disclosure a non-profit owes a sponsor. Core idea: the headset gets passed around.
